goals: Name alkynes and describe the sp hybridised, linear triple bond of ethyne
Prepare ethyne from calcium carbide and from natural gas, and alkynes by dehydrohalogenation and Kolbe electrolysis
Explain the acidic character of terminal alkynes and write the formation of acetylides

slides.heading: Alkynes: hydrocarbons with a C≡C bond
slides.body_md: **Alkynes** are unsaturated hydrocarbons that contain **one carbon–carbon triple bond**; general formula **CₙH₂ₙ₋₂**. The first member, ethyne, is also called **acetylene**. Alkynes are more unsaturated than alkenes (two π bonds) but, as we shall see, react more slowly with electrophiles.

visual.alt: Table of five alkynes with formula, boiling point in degrees Celsius and state at 298 kelvin

slides.narration: Welcome to the chapter on alkynes. Alkynes are hydrocarbons with one carbon carbon triple bond. Their general formula is C n H two n minus two, which is two hydrogens fewer than the alkene with the same number of carbons. The simplest alkyne, ethyne, is also called acetylene. The first three members are gases and the higher ones are liquids. In this part we study structure, preparation and the acidic character of the terminal hydrogen.

slides.heading: Naming alkynes
slides.body_md: (1) Choose the **longest chain that contains the triple bond**; change **-ane to -yne**. (2) Number from the end that gives the **triple bond the lowest locant**. (3) Write the locant before "-yne". (4) Name and number the substituents as for alkanes. A compound with both bonds is an **-en-yne**: give the lowest locants to the multiple bonds together, and the double bond the lower number if there is a choice. Alkynes with a **terminal** ≡C–H are called terminal alkynes.

visual.alt: Table of seven alkynes with their structural formula and IUPAC name

slides.narration: To name an alkyne, take the longest chain that includes the triple bond and change the ending from ane to yne. Number the chain so that the triple bond gets the lowest possible number. For example, the four carbon alkyne with the bond at the end is but one yne, and with the bond in the middle is but two yne. A compound with both a double and a triple bond is named as an ene yne, and the double bond gets the lower number if there is a choice.

slides.heading: Structure of the triple bond in ethyne
slides.body_md: Each carbon of ethyne is **sp hybridised**: two sp orbitals (50% s character) form σ bonds, one to the other carbon and one to hydrogen, on a **straight line (H–C–C = 180°)**. The two remaining **p orbitals** on each carbon overlap sideways in two perpendicular planes to give **two π bonds**. So $\ce{C#C}$ is **one σ + two π**; the molecule has **3 σ and 2 π bonds**. **C≡C is 120 pm** (C=C 134 pm, C–C 154 pm), C–H is 106 pm.

slides.narration: In ethyne each carbon atom is sp hybridised. The two hybrid orbitals make sigma bonds, one to hydrogen and one to the other carbon, and they point in opposite directions, so the molecule is a straight line with a bond angle of one hundred and eighty degrees. The two unhybridised p orbitals on each carbon overlap sideways in two planes at right angles, forming two pi bonds. The triple bond is therefore one sigma and two pi bonds, and it is very short.

slides.heading: Isomerism in alkynes
slides.body_md: Alkynes show **position isomerism** (but-1-yne and but-2-yne) and **chain isomerism** (pent-1-yne and 3-methylbut-1-yne). **No cis–trans isomerism** occurs about C≡C: each triple-bonded carbon has only one other group, on a straight line. C₄H₆ has **2** alkynes and C₅H₈ has **3**. Alkynes are also **functional isomers** of alkadienes and cycloalkenes (C₄H₆: buta-1,3-diene and cyclobutene).

slides.narration: Alkynes show position isomerism, as in but one yne and but two yne, and chain isomerism, as in pent one yne and three methylbut one yne. They do not show cis trans isomerism, because each carbon of the triple bond carries only one other group and the four atoms lie on a straight line. Four carbon alkynes number two and five carbon alkynes number three. Alkynes are also functional isomers of dienes and of cyclic alkenes.

slides.heading: Physical properties of alkynes
slides.body_md: Alkynes are **colourless**, non-polar or very weakly polar, **insoluble in water** but soluble in organic solvents (ethyne dissolves well in propanone, so cylinders hold it dissolved in propanone). Their **boiling points are a little higher than those of the alkene and alkane with the same carbon number**: the linear shape packs closely and the π electrons are easily polarised. Pure ethyne is almost odourless; the garlic-like smell of the carbide gas is due to traces of phosphine.

visual.alt: Table comparing boiling points of alkane, alkene and alkyne with four, five and six carbons

slides.narration: Alkynes are colourless and almost non polar, so they do not dissolve in water but dissolve in organic solvents. Ethyne is very soluble in propanone, and welding cylinders contain it dissolved in propanone for safety. The boiling points of alkynes are slightly higher than those of the alkene and the alkane with the same number of carbons, because the straight molecules pack closely and the pi electrons are easily polarised.

slides.heading: Preparation of alkynes: the main routes
slides.body_md: Ethyne is made industrially from **calcium carbide** and from **natural gas (methane)**. Alkynes are made in the laboratory by **double dehydrohalogenation** of vicinal or geminal dihalides with alcoholic KOH (then NaNH₂) and, for ethyne, by **Kolbe electrolysis** of potassium maleate or fumarate.

visual.alt: Table of five routes to ethyne and alkynes with reagents and products

slides.narration: Here are the main routes. Industrially ethyne comes from calcium carbide and water, and from methane in natural gas. In the laboratory a dihalide, with halogens on neighbouring carbons or on the same carbon, loses two molecules of hydrogen halide with alcoholic potassium hydroxide, and the product is an alkyne. Ethyne can also be made by the Kolbe electrolysis of potassium fumarate or maleate.

slides.heading: Ethyne from calcium carbide
slides.body_md: Limestone gives lime; lime and coke in an **electric arc furnace (about 2273 K)** give **calcium carbide**; carbide reacts with cold water to give **ethyne** and slaked lime. $\ce{CaC2 + 2H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2}$. Commercial ethyne contains traces of H₂S, PH₃ and NH₃ from impurities in the coke; they are removed by washing with acidified copper(II) sulphate solution.

slides.narration: Limestone is heated to give lime. Lime is heated with coke in an electric arc furnace at about two thousand two hundred and seventy three kelvin to give calcium carbide and carbon monoxide. When calcium carbide meets water, ethyne gas bubbles out and slaked lime remains. Traces of hydrogen sulphide, phosphine and ammonia come from impurities in the coke, and they are removed by washing the gas with acidified copper sulphate solution.

slides.heading: Worked example: ethyne from carbide
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A volunteer drops 6.40 g of pure calcium carbide into excess water. Find the volume of ethyne at STP and the mass of calcium hydroxide formed. (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16, H = 1; molar volume 22.4 L.)

**Solution.** $\ce{CaC2 + 2H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2}$. M(CaC₂) = 64 g mol⁻¹, so n = 6.40 ÷ 64 = 0.100 mol. The ratio is 1 : 1 : 1, so V(C₂H₂) = 0.100 × 22.4 = **2.24 L**, and m[Ca(OH)₂] = 0.100 × 74 = **7.40 g**.

visual.alt: Table of moles of calcium carbide, volume of ethyne at STP and mass of calcium hydroxide

slides.narration: Write the balanced equation first. One mole of calcium carbide gives one mole of ethyne and one mole of calcium hydroxide. The molar mass of calcium carbide is sixty four grams per mole, so six point four grams is point one zero zero mole. That mole amount of ethyne occupies point one zero zero times twenty two point four litres at standard temperature and pressure, and the same amount of calcium hydroxide has a mass found by multiplying by its molar mass of seventy four.

slides.heading: Natural gas, dihalides and Kolbe electrolysis
slides.body_md: **Natural gas:** methane heated in an electric arc to about 1773 K for a fraction of a second, then quenched: $\ce{2CH4 -> C2H2 + 3H2}$; or by **partial oxidation** with oxygen: $\ce{6CH4 + O2 -> 2C2H2 + 2CO + 10H2}$. **Dihalides:** $\ce{CH2BrCH2Br + 2KOH -> HC#CH + 2KBr + 2H2O}$ (alcoholic KOH; the second HBr often needs NaNH₂). A **geminal** dihalide such as $\ce{CH3CHBr2}$ reacts in the same way.

visual.alt: Table of starting materials, reagents and alkyne products for natural gas and dihalide routes

slides.narration: In the natural gas route, methane is heated in an electric arc to about one thousand seven hundred and seventy three kelvin for a very short time and then cooled quickly, and ethyne and hydrogen form. Partial oxidation with a limited supply of oxygen gives ethyne too. In the laboratory, a dihalide loses two molecules of hydrogen halide. The halogens can be on neighbouring carbons, which is vicinal, or on the same carbon, which is geminal.

slides.heading: Kolbe's electrolysis of potassium fumarate
slides.body_md: Electrolysis of a concentrated aqueous solution of **potassium maleate or fumarate** gives **ethyne at the anode**: each carboxylate loses CO₂ and the two remaining CH carbons join by a triple bond. $\ce{KOOCCH=CHCOOK + 2H2O -> HC#CH + 2CO2 + H2 + 2KOH}$. At the cathode, hydrogen is liberated and the solution becomes alkaline. (Potassium succinate gives ethene in the same way.)

visual.alt: Electrolysis of aqueous potassium fumarate gives ethyne and carbon dioxide at the anode, and hydrogen and potassium hydroxide at the cathode
visual.caption: Kolbe electrolysis giving ethyne

slides.narration: In the Kolbe method, a concentrated solution of potassium fumarate or potassium maleate is electrolysed. At the anode the two carboxylate groups are lost as carbon dioxide and the two carbons left behind join by a triple bond, so ethyne is liberated. At the cathode, hydrogen is given off and potassium hydroxide builds up in the solution. Potassium succinate, with a saturated chain, gives ethene by the same change.

slides.heading: Why terminal alkynes are acidic
slides.body_md: The C–H bond of ethyne uses an **sp orbital (50% s character)**, compared with 33% in ethene and 25% in ethane. An s orbital is nearer the nucleus, so an sp carbon is **more electronegative** and holds the bonding pair more tightly: the hydrogen is released as H⁺ more easily and the **acetylide ion HC≡C⁻** is stabilised. Ethyne is a weak acid (pKa about 25), far stronger than ethene (about 44) and ethane (about 50), but it is **weaker than water**.

slides.narration: The carbon hydrogen bond in ethyne uses an sp orbital, which has fifty percent s character, against thirty three percent in ethene and twenty five percent in ethane. An s orbital lies closer to the nucleus, so the carbon holds the bonding pair more tightly and behaves as though it were more electronegative. The hydrogen is lost as a proton more easily, and the acetylide ion is stabilised. So ethyne is a much stronger acid than ethene or ethane, although it is still weaker than water.

slides.heading: Formation of acetylides
slides.body_md: Terminal alkynes (≡C–H) form **metal acetylides**; internal alkynes (no ≡C–H) do not. **Sodium:** $\ce{2HC#CH + 2Na -> 2HC#CNa + H2}$. **Sodium amide** (liquid NH₃): $\ce{HC#CH + NaNH2 -> HC#CNa + NH3}$. **Ammoniacal silver nitrate** gives a **white precipitate** of silver acetylide and **ammoniacal cuprous chloride** a **red precipitate** of copper acetylide: $\ce{HC#CH + 2AgNO3 + 2NH4OH -> AgC#CAg + 2NH4NO3 + 2H2O}$. Dry heavy-metal acetylides explode on shock; dilute HNO₃ regenerates the alkyne.

visual.alt: Table comparing the reactions of a terminal alkyne and an internal alkyne with sodium, ammoniacal silver nitrate and ammoniacal cuprous chloride

slides.narration: A terminal alkyne, with a hydrogen on the triple bonded carbon, loses that hydrogen to a strong base or to a metal. Sodium or sodium amide gives sodium acetylide. Ammoniacal silver nitrate gives a white precipitate of silver acetylide, and ammoniacal cuprous chloride gives a red precipitate of copper acetylide. An internal alkyne has no such hydrogen and gives no precipitate. Dry heavy metal acetylides explode on shock, so they are destroyed with dilute nitric acid.

slides.heading: Worked example: which alkynes form acetylides?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Pent-1-yne, pent-2-yne and 3-methylbut-1-yne are tested with ammoniacal silver nitrate. Which give a precipitate, and why?

**Solution.** A precipitate needs a **≡C–H** group. Pent-1-yne, $\ce{CH3CH2CH2C#CH}$, and 3-methylbut-1-yne, $\ce{(CH3)2CHC#CH}$, are **terminal** alkynes and give a **white precipitate**. Pent-2-yne, $\ce{CH3C#CCH2CH3}$, has no hydrogen on a triple-bonded carbon and gives **none**. The test therefore separates terminal from internal alkynes, not one terminal alkyne from another.

visual.alt: Table of three C5H8 alkynes showing whether each has a terminal hydrogen and whether it gives a precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate

slides.narration: Look for a hydrogen on a triple bonded carbon. Pent one yne and three methylbut one yne both end in a triple bond with a hydrogen, so both give a white precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate. Pent two yne has the triple bond inside the chain, with no such hydrogen, so nothing happens. The test tells terminal alkynes from internal ones, but it cannot tell two terminal alkynes apart.

slides.heading: Addition reactions of alkynes
slides.body_md: The triple bond has **two π bonds**, so an alkyne can add **two molecules** of a reagent: first it becomes an alkene derivative, then a saturated compound. Alkynes are attacked by **electrophiles**, though more slowly than alkenes because the sp carbons hold the π electrons more tightly and the intermediate (a vinyl cation) is less stable.

visual.alt: Table of the first and second addition products of ethyne with hydrogen, bromine, hydrogen chloride and water

slides.narration: An alkyne has two pi bonds, so it can add two molecules of a reagent. The first addition gives an alkene derivative, and the second gives a saturated compound. Alkynes react with electrophiles, but more slowly than alkenes, because the sp hybridised carbons hold the pi electrons more tightly. In this part we study addition of hydrogen, halogens, hydrogen halides and water, then oxidation, polymerisation, uses and tests.

slides.heading: Addition of hydrogen
slides.body_md: With **H₂ and Ni (or Pt, Pd)** an alkyne is reduced fully to the alkane: $\ce{HC#CH + 2H2 -> CH3CH3}$. To **stop at the alkene**, use **Lindlar's catalyst** (Pd on CaCO₃, poisoned with lead acetate and quinoline), which gives the **cis** alkene by syn addition, or **sodium in liquid ammonia**, which gives the **trans** alkene by anti addition.

slides.narration: With hydrogen and nickel, platinum or palladium, an alkyne takes up two molecules of hydrogen and becomes an alkane. To stop at the alkene, the catalyst must be chosen. Lindlar catalyst is palladium on calcium carbonate, poisoned with lead acetate and quinoline. It adds both hydrogens on the same side and gives the cis alkene. Sodium in liquid ammonia adds the hydrogens on opposite sides and gives the trans alkene.

slides.heading: Addition of halogens
slides.body_md: **Bromine or chlorine** adds twice. Ethyne with bromine in CCl₄ gives **1,2-dibromoethene** and then **1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane**: $\ce{HC#CH + 2Br2 -> CHBr2CHBr2}$. The **red-brown colour of bromine water is lost**, a test for unsaturation (the decolourisation is slower than with alkenes). Chlorine with ethyne is explosive unless a catalyst such as FeCl₃ or a solvent is used.

visual.alt: Ethyne with one mole of bromine gives 1,2-dibromoethene
visual.caption: Step 1 of the double addition; step 2 gives CHBr₂CHBr₂

slides.narration: Bromine adds to ethyne in two steps. The first mole gives one two dibromoethene, and the second mole gives one one two two tetrabromoethane. The red brown colour of bromine is lost, which is the usual test for unsaturation, although the colour fades more slowly than with an alkene. Chlorine reacts violently with ethyne unless a catalyst or a solvent is used to moderate the reaction.

slides.heading: Addition of hydrogen halides: Markownikoff's rule twice
slides.body_md: HX adds in two steps, each following **Markownikoff's rule**, so the second halogen goes on the **same carbon** as the first (a **geminal** dihalide). $\ce{HC#CH + HCl -> CH2=CHCl}$ (HgCl₂, 333–343 K; chloroethene, the monomer of PVC), then $\ce{CH2=CHCl + HCl -> CH3CHCl2}$. Propyne with excess HBr gives **2,2-dibromopropane**.

visual.alt: Table of the products of adding one and two moles of hydrogen halide to ethyne, propyne and but-1-yne

slides.narration: Hydrogen halides add to an alkyne in two steps, and each step follows Markownikoff rule. Ethyne with one mole of hydrogen chloride gives chloroethene, the monomer of polyvinyl chloride. A second mole adds to the same carbon, giving one one dichloroethane, a geminal dihalide. In the same way propyne with excess hydrogen bromide gives two two dibromopropane, with both bromines on the middle carbon.

slides.body_md: Apply Markownikoff's rule twice; both halogens end up on one carbon.
slides.narration: Quick check. Add the first molecule by Markownikoff rule, then add the second to the carbon that already carries the halogen.

slides.heading: Addition of water: hydration
slides.body_md: Alkynes add water in the presence of **HgSO₄ and dilute H₂SO₄ (about 333 K)**. The first product is an **enol** (OH on a C=C), which is unstable and shifts at once to the **carbonyl** form (**tautomerism**). Ethyne gives **ethanal**; **propyne** gives **propanone**, because OH adds by Markownikoff's rule to the carbon with fewer hydrogens. **Every alkyne except ethyne therefore gives a ketone.**

slides.narration: In hydration, water adds to the alkyne in the presence of mercuric sulphate and dilute sulphuric acid. The first product is an enol, a compound with a hydroxyl group on a double bonded carbon. An enol is unstable and shifts at once to the carbonyl form, which is called tautomerism. Ethyne gives ethanal, which is an aldehyde. Propyne gives propanone, because the hydroxyl goes to the carbon with fewer hydrogens. Every other alkyne gives a ketone.

slides.heading: Worked example: predicting the hydration product
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give the product of hydration of (a) but-1-yne and (b) but-2-yne, using HgSO₄ and dilute H₂SO₄.

**Solution.** (a) OH goes to C-2 (the carbon with fewer H): the enol $\ce{CH2=C(OH)CH2CH3}$ becomes **butanone**, $\ce{CH3COCH2CH3}$. (b) But-2-yne is symmetrical, so both carbons are alike: the enol $\ce{CH3CH=C(OH)CH3}$ also becomes **butanone**. Both alkynes give the **same ketone**; the carbonyl carbon is the one that held the OH.

visual.alt: Table of the enol and final carbonyl product from the hydration of but-1-yne, but-2-yne and ethyne

slides.narration: Put the hydroxyl group on the carbon that has fewer hydrogens. In but one yne that is carbon two, so the enol shifts to butanone. But two yne is symmetrical, so either carbon receives the hydroxyl, and the enol again shifts to butanone. The two different alkynes therefore give the same ketone. Only ethyne, which has no carbon with fewer hydrogens to choose, gives an aldehyde.

slides.heading: Oxidation: combustion and potassium permanganate
slides.body_md: **Combustion:** $\ce{2C2H2 + 5O2 -> 4CO2 + 2H2O}$; the **oxy-acetylene flame** reaches about 3000 °C and is used for welding and cutting steel. **Hot alkaline or acidified KMnO₄** cleaves the triple bond: $\ce{R-C#C-R}$ gives **2 RCOOH**; a terminal alkyne gives RCOOH and CO₂. The purple colour of cold dilute permanganate is also lost with alkynes, which is why Baeyer's test cannot separate alkenes from alkynes.

visual.alt: Table of products of oxidation of four alkynes with hot potassium permanganate

slides.narration: Alkynes burn to carbon dioxide and water. Ethyne burnt in oxygen gives the oxy acetylene flame, one of the hottest chemical flames, at about three thousand degrees Celsius, used to weld and cut steel. Hot potassium permanganate breaks the triple bond, and each carbon of the triple bond becomes a carboxylic acid group. A terminal alkyne also gives carbon dioxide from the end carbon. Cold dilute permanganate is also decolourised by alkynes.

slides.heading: Ozonolysis of alkynes
slides.body_md: Ozone adds to the triple bond; the ozonide, on hydrolysis, gives **1,2-dicarbonyl compounds** (or, with oxidising work-up, **carboxylic acids**). Ethyne gives **glyoxal (ethanedial)**, OHC–CHO. Working back from the products, the two carbons that were bonded by the triple bond are the carbonyl carbons that were **joined to each other**.

visual.alt: Table of ozonolysis and permanganate products of ethyne, but-2-yne and hex-3-yne

slides.narration: Ozone adds across the triple bond, and the ozonide formed is split by water. Ethyne gives glyoxal, which is the dialdehyde ethanedial. An internal alkyne gives a one two diketone, and with an oxidising work up or with hot permanganate the product is a pair of carboxylic acids. To find an alkyne from such products, join the two carbonyl carbons that were linked, and remove the oxygen atoms.

slides.heading: Polymerisation of ethyne
slides.body_md: **Cyclic polymerisation:** ethyne passed through a **red-hot iron tube (873 K)** trimerises to **benzene**: $\ce{3C2H2 -> C6H6}$. Propyne gives 1,3,5-trimethylbenzene. **Linear polymerisation:** two molecules with Cu₂Cl₂/NH₄Cl give **vinylacetylene**, used for neoprene rubber; many molecules give **polyacetylene**, a conducting polymer.

slides.narration: When ethyne is passed through a red hot iron tube at about eight hundred and seventy three kelvin, three molecules join to form a ring of benzene. This is cyclic polymerisation. Propyne treated in the same way gives one three five trimethylbenzene. Linear polymerisation is also possible. Two molecules with cuprous chloride and ammonium chloride give vinylacetylene, used to make neoprene, and many molecules give polyacetylene, a polymer that conducts electricity.

slides.heading: Uses of alkynes and the flame test
slides.body_md: Ethyne is used for **oxy-acetylene welding and cutting**, and as the starting material for **ethanal and ethanoic acid**, **chloroethene (PVC)**, **neoprene**, and the solvent 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane. It burns with a **sooty, luminous flame in air** because its carbon content is high: the percentage of carbon is **92.3% in ethyne**, 85.7% in ethene and 80.0% in ethane.

visual.alt: Table of percentage of carbon and flame appearance for ethane, ethene and ethyne

slides.narration: Ethyne is used in oxy acetylene welding and cutting, and as a raw material for ethanal, ethanoic acid, chloroethene for polyvinyl chloride, neoprene rubber and the solvent tetrachloroethane. In air it burns with a sooty luminous flame, because the share of carbon is very high, about ninety two percent. Ethene has less carbon and burns with a smoky flame, and ethane burns with an almost clear flame.

slides.heading: Distinguishing ethane, ethene and ethyne
slides.body_md: Two reagents are enough. **Ammoniacal AgNO₃ (or Cu₂Cl₂)** gives a precipitate **only with a terminal alkyne**. **Bromine water** (or Baeyer's reagent) is decolourised by **both alkenes and alkynes** but not by alkanes. So: pass the gas through ammoniacal silver nitrate (precipitate = ethyne); then test the rest with bromine water (decolourised = ethene; no change = ethane).

nodes.label: Unknown gas: ethane, ethene or ethyne
No precipitate: shake with bromine water

visual.alt: Decision tree for telling ethane, ethene and ethyne apart: silver nitrate first, then bromine water

slides.narration: To tell ethane, ethene and ethyne apart, use two reagents in order. First pass the gas through ammoniacal silver nitrate. A white precipitate shows ethyne, because only a terminal alkyne has an acidic hydrogen. If there is no precipitate, shake the gas with bromine water. If the colour is lost, the gas is ethene, and if nothing happens it is ethane. Bromine water or Baeyer reagent alone cannot separate an alkene from an alkyne.

slides.heading: Worked example: analysing a gas mixture
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 60.0 mL of a mixture of ethene and ethyne is shaken with ammoniacal silver nitrate. The volume of gas left is 38.0 mL. Find the percentage of ethyne by volume, and the volume of H₂ needed to hydrogenate the original mixture fully (Ni, excess H₂).

**Solution.** Only ethyne forms a precipitate, so V(ethene) = 38.0 mL and V(ethyne) = 60.0 − 38.0 = **22.0 mL**, i.e. 22.0 ÷ 60.0 × 100 = **36.7%**. Ethene takes 1 H₂ and ethyne takes 2 H₂: V(H₂) = 38.0 + 2 × 22.0 = **82.0 mL**.

visual.alt: Table of the volumes of ethene and ethyne in the mixture and the volume of hydrogen each needs for complete hydrogenation

slides.narration: The silver nitrate absorbs only ethyne, so the gas that remains is ethene. The difference between the original volume and the remaining volume is the ethyne. Dividing by the original volume and multiplying by one hundred gives the percentage of ethyne. For hydrogenation, ethene needs one volume of hydrogen for each volume, and ethyne needs two, so the total is the ethene volume plus twice the ethyne volume.

sections.heading: 1. Nomenclature, isomerism and the triple bond
sections.body_md: **Alkynes** are unsaturated hydrocarbons with one C≡C bond; general formula **CₙH₂ₙ₋₂**. **Naming:** longest chain containing the triple bond; change **-ane to -yne**; the triple bond gets the **lowest locant** (but-1-yne, pent-2-yne, 4-methylhex-2-yne); with a double bond too, the name ends **-en-yne**. **Isomerism:** position and chain isomerism only (C₄H₆: 2 alkynes; C₅H₈: 3); **no cis–trans** isomerism because the triple-bonded carbons carry one group each on a straight line. **Structure of ethyne:** each carbon is **sp hybridised** (two sp orbitals, 50% s); the molecule is **linear (180°)**; the bond is **one σ and two π** (two perpendicular π clouds); **C≡C 120 pm**, C–H 106 pm; ethyne has 3 σ and 2 π bonds. Bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): C–C 347, C=C 611, C≡C 837, so the second π bond (226) is weaker than the first (264).

key_terms.definition_md: An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing one carbon–carbon triple bond.
An alkyne with the triple bond at the end of the chain, so that one triple-bonded carbon carries a hydrogen (≡C–H).
Mixing of one s and one p orbital to give two orbitals at 180°, each with 50% s character.

sections.heading: 2. Physical properties
sections.body_md: Alkynes are colourless, non-polar or very weakly polar, **insoluble in water**, soluble in organic solvents; ethyne is **very soluble in propanone** (cylinders hold it dissolved in propanone on a porous filler). C₂–C₄ are gases (ethyne sublimes at −84 °C); higher members are liquids. **Boiling points are slightly higher than those of the alkene and alkane with the same carbon number** (but-1-yne 8.1 °C, but-1-ene −6.3 °C, butane −0.5 °C; pent-1-yne 40.2 °C, pentane 36.1 °C), because the linear molecules pack closely and the π electrons are easily polarised. The boiling point rises with chain length; a terminal alkyne boils lower than the internal isomer (but-1-yne 8.1 °C, but-2-yne 27.0 °C).

key_terms.definition_md: Change of a solid directly into a gas; ethyne at 1 atm turns from solid to gas at −84 °C.

sections.heading: 4. Acidic character and acetylides
sections.body_md: The C–H of a terminal alkyne uses an **sp orbital (50% s)**; the orbital is close to the nucleus, so the carbon is relatively electronegative, the proton is released more easily and **HC≡C⁻ is stabilised**. Approximate pKa: ethyne 25, ethene 44, ethane 50, so the order of acidity is **ethyne > ethene > ethane** (the order of s character). Ethyne is weaker than water and alcohols. **Acetylides:** 2HC≡CH + 2Na → 2HC≡CNa + H₂; HC≡CH + NaNH₂ → HC≡CNa + NH₃; with **ammoniacal silver nitrate** a **white** precipitate of silver acetylide; with **ammoniacal cuprous chloride** a **red** precipitate of copper acetylide. Only **terminal** alkynes react; but-2-yne does not. Dry heavy-metal acetylides explode; dilute HNO₃ regenerates the alkyne.

sections.body_md: **H₂:** with Ni, Pt or Pd to the alkane (HC≡CH + 2H₂ → CH₃CH₃); with **Lindlar's catalyst** (Pd/CaCO₃, poisoned with Pb(OAc)₂/quinoline) the **cis alkene** (syn addition); with **Na in liquid NH₃** the **trans alkene** (anti addition). **Halogens** add twice (1,2-dihaloalkene then 1,1,2,2-tetrahaloalkane); bromine water is decolourised, more slowly than by an alkene. **HX** adds twice by **Markownikoff's rule**, giving a **geminal** dihalide (HC≡CH + HCl → CH₂=CHCl → CH₃CHCl₂; propyne + 2HBr → 2,2-dibromopropane); chloroethene is the monomer of PVC. **Water** (HgSO₄, dilute H₂SO₄, about 333 K): enol, then carbonyl by **tautomerism**; ethyne gives **ethanal**, propyne gives **propanone**, every other alkyne a ketone.

sections.heading: 6. Oxidation, ozonolysis, polymerisation and uses
sections.body_md: **Combustion:** 2C₂H₂ + 5O₂ → 4CO₂ + 2H₂O; sooty flame in air (92.3% carbon), very hot **oxy-acetylene flame (about 3000 °C)** in oxygen, used for welding. **Hot KMnO₄** cleaves C≡C to carboxylic acids (R–C≡C–R gives 2RCOOH; a terminal alkyne gives RCOOH and CO₂); cold dilute KMnO₄ is also decolourised. **Ozonolysis** gives 1,2-dicarbonyl compounds (ethyne gives glyoxal, OHC–CHO). **Polymerisation:** 3C₂H₂ → C₆H₆ through a **red-hot iron tube at 873 K** (propyne gives 1,3,5-trimethylbenzene); linear: vinylacetylene (Cu₂Cl₂, NH₄Cl) and **polyacetylene**. **Uses:** oxy-acetylene welding; ethanal and ethanoic acid; chloroethene (PVC); neoprene; tetrachloroethane solvent.

sections.heading: 7. Distinguishing alkanes, alkenes and alkynes
sections.body_md: **Ammoniacal AgNO₃** (white precipitate) or **ammoniacal Cu₂Cl₂** (red precipitate): **only terminal alkynes**. **Bromine water** (or bromine in CCl₄) and **Baeyer's reagent** (cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄): decolourised by **alkenes and alkynes**, not by alkanes. Scheme: ethane, ethene and ethyne → ammoniacal AgNO₃: precipitate = ethyne; the others → bromine water: decolourised = ethene, no change = ethane. But-1-yne and but-2-yne are separated by ammoniacal AgNO₃ (precipitate with but-1-yne only).

key_terms.definition_md: Cold, dilute, alkaline potassium permanganate; decolourised by alkenes and alkynes.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling the triple bond "one σ and one π" (it is one σ and two π), or the molecule bent (ethyne is linear, 180°).
- Writing cis–trans isomers for an alkyne (none exist).
- Forgetting that a dihalide needs two moles of KOH, or that HX and X₂ add twice (geminal and tetrahalo products).
- Giving propanal for the hydration of propyne (the product is propanone) or an aldehyde from any alkyne except ethyne.
- Saying bromine water separates ethene from ethyne (both decolourise it; use ammoniacal AgNO₃).
- Claiming that all alkynes react with silver nitrate (only terminal ones).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Structure: hybridisation, σ and π count, angle and bond length.
- Preparation and reactions: balanced equation with the reagent and condition.
- Acidity: 50% s character, stability of the acetylide ion, comparison with ethene and ethane.
- Tests: reagent, observation and conclusion for each compound.

cards.front_md: General formula of alkynes?
cards.back_md: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (one C≡C bond).

cards.front_md: How are alkynes named?
cards.back_md: Longest chain containing C≡C; -ane becomes -yne; lowest locant for the triple bond.

cards.front_md: Hybridisation and shape of ethyne?
cards.back_md: sp; linear, H–C–C = 180°.

cards.front_md: Bonds in the C≡C bond?
cards.back_md: One σ (sp–sp) and two π (p–p, in perpendicular planes).

cards.front_md: Length of C≡C in ethyne?
cards.back_md: About 120 pm (C=C 134 pm; C–C 154 pm).

cards.front_md: Number of σ and π bonds in ethyne?
cards.back_md: 3 σ and 2 π.

cards.front_md: Why do alkynes show no cis–trans isomerism?
cards.back_md: Each triple-bonded carbon has only one other group, on a straight line.

cards.front_md: Number of alkynes of formula C₄H₆ and C₅H₈?
cards.back_md: 2 and 3.

cards.front_md: Compare boiling points of alkane, alkene and alkyne of equal carbon number.
cards.back_md: Alkyne highest (linear shape, polarisable π electrons); alkene lowest of the three for C₄ and C₅ (but-1-yne 8.1, but-1-ene −6.3, butane −0.5 °C).

cards.front_md: In which solvent is ethyne stored in cylinders?
cards.back_md: Dissolved in propanone on a porous filler (very soluble in propanone).

cards.front_md: Laboratory source of ethyne and equation?
cards.back_md: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ + Ca(OH)₂.

cards.front_md: How is calcium carbide made?
cards.back_md: CaO + 3C → CaC₂ + CO in an electric furnace at about 2273 K.

cards.front_md: Impurities in carbide ethyne and their removal?
cards.back_md: H₂S, PH₃, NH₃; washed out with acidified copper(II) sulphate solution.

cards.front_md: Ethyne from natural gas?
cards.back_md: 2CH₄ → C₂H₂ + 3H₂ in an electric arc at about 1773 K, then rapid quenching; or partial oxidation.

cards.front_md: Dihalide to alkyne: reagent and moles?
cards.back_md: Alcoholic KOH, 2 mol (then NaNH₂ if needed); vicinal or geminal dihalide.

cards.front_md: Kolbe's method for ethyne?
cards.back_md: Electrolysis of aqueous potassium maleate or fumarate: ethyne and CO₂ at the anode.

cards.front_md: Why is ethyne acidic?
cards.back_md: The C–H bond uses an sp orbital (50% s), making carbon more electronegative and stabilising HC≡C⁻.

cards.front_md: Order of acidity of C–H in ethane, ethene, ethyne?
cards.back_md: Ethyne > ethene > ethane (pKa about 25, 44, 50).

cards.front_md: Test for a terminal alkyne with silver?
cards.back_md: Ammoniacal AgNO₃ gives a white precipitate of silver acetylide.

cards.front_md: Test for a terminal alkyne with copper?
cards.back_md: Ammoniacal Cu₂Cl₂ gives a red precipitate of copper acetylide.

cards.front_md: Ethyne with NaNH₂?
cards.back_md: HC≡CH + NaNH₂ → HC≡CNa + NH₃ (sodium acetylide).

cards.front_md: Why does but-2-yne give no acetylide?
cards.back_md: It has no hydrogen on a triple-bonded carbon.

cards.front_md: Ethyne + excess H₂ (Ni)?
cards.back_md: Ethane (two moles of H₂ per mole of ethyne).

cards.front_md: Alkyne to cis alkene; to trans alkene?
cards.back_md: H₂ with Lindlar catalyst; Na in liquid NH₃.

cards.front_md: Ethyne + 2Br₂?
cards.back_md: 1,1,2,2-Tetrabromoethane, CHBr₂CHBr₂.

cards.front_md: Propyne + 2HBr?
cards.back_md: 2,2-Dibromopropane (Markownikoff twice, geminal).

cards.front_md: Hydration of ethyne: reagents and product?
cards.back_md: HgSO₄, dilute H₂SO₄: ethenol (enol) → ethanal.

cards.front_md: Hydration of propyne gives?
cards.back_md: Propanone (by Markownikoff addition and tautomerism).

cards.front_md: Hot KMnO₄ with R–C≡C–R?
cards.back_md: Two molecules of RCOOH.

cards.front_md: Cyclic polymerisation of ethyne?
cards.back_md: 3C₂H₂ → C₆H₆ in a red-hot iron tube at 873 K.

cards.front_md: Why does ethyne burn with a sooty flame?
cards.back_md: High carbon content (92.3%), so combustion is incomplete in air.

cards.front_md: How to distinguish ethane, ethene and ethyne?
cards.back_md: Ammoniacal AgNO₃ precipitate = ethyne; the rest with bromine water: decolourised = ethene, no change = ethane.

questions.stem_md: A perfumer's assistant draws the structure CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂C≡CCH₃ for a hydrocarbon found in a floral extract. Its IUPAC name is:
questions.solution_md: The longest chain containing C≡C has 6 carbons. Numbering from the CH₃–C≡ end gives the triple bond locant 2 (from the other end it would be 4), so the methyl group is on C-5: 5-methylhex-2-yne, option (a). Option (b) numbers from the wrong end, (c) puts the methyl on the wrong carbon and (d) gives the triple bond the wrong locant.

questions.stem_md: In a molecule of but-1-yne, HC≡C–CH₂–CH₃, the hybridisation of the four carbon atoms, taken from the ≡CH end, is:
questions.solution_md: The two carbons of the triple bond each have two σ bonds and two π bonds, so they are sp; the CH₂ and CH₃ carbons have four σ bonds each, so sp³. The order is sp, sp, sp³, sp³ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student counts the bonds in one molecule of 3-methylbut-1-yne, (CH₃)₂CH–C≡CH. The numbers of σ bonds and π bonds are respectively:
questions.solution_md: The molecule C₅H₈ has 13 atoms joined in an open chain, so it has 12 σ bonds (8 C–H and 4 C–C, the triple bond contributing one σ). The triple bond has two π bonds. So 12 σ and 2 π — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student lists every open-chain structural isomer of C₅H₈ that contains one carbon–carbon triple bond and no other multiple bond. The number of such isomers is:
questions.solution_md: The isomers are pent-1-yne, pent-2-yne and 3-methylbut-1-yne: 3 in all — option (b). No alkyne has cis–trans isomers, so the count cannot rise to (c) or (d), and 2 (a) misses the branched isomer.

questions.stem_md: The average bond enthalpies of C–C, C=C and C≡C are 347, 611 and 837 kJ mol⁻¹ respectively. The energy contributed by the second π bond, the extra enthalpy gained when a C=C bond becomes a C≡C bond, is:
questions.solution_md: Second π bond = 837 − 611 = 226 kJ mol⁻¹ — option (a). The first π bond is 611 − 347 = 264 kJ mol⁻¹ (b), so the second π bond is weaker than the first; 490 kJ mol⁻¹ (c) is the two π bonds together and 837 (d) is the whole triple bond.

questions.stem_md: In a school laboratory the teacher needs a gas jar of ethyne quickly and cheaply. The pair of reactants that gives ethyne directly is:

options.text_md: ethanol and concentrated sulphuric acid at 443 K

questions.solution_md: Calcium carbide with cold water gives ethyne and calcium hydroxide, CaC₂ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ + Ca(OH)₂ — option (c). Sodium ethanoate with soda lime gives methane (a), ethanol with hot conc. H₂SO₄ gives ethene (b) and bromoethane with aqueous KOH gives ethanol (d).

questions.stem_md: A technician heats 1,1-dichloropropane with a large excess of alcoholic potassium hydroxide. The organic product is:
questions.solution_md: A geminal dihalide loses two molecules of HCl with alcoholic KOH, forming a triple bond: CH₃CH₂CHCl₂ gives CH₃C≡CH, propyne — option (a). Loss of only one HCl would give a chloropropene; propene (b) and propane (c) would need reduction and propan-1-ol (d) forms with aqueous KOH.

questions.stem_md: A concentrated aqueous solution of potassium maleate, KOOC–CH=CH–COOK, is electrolysed between platinum electrodes. Besides carbon dioxide, the hydrocarbon formed at the anode is:
questions.solution_md: Each carboxylate group is lost as CO₂ and the two remaining =CH– carbons are joined by a triple bond: ⁻OOC–CH=CH–COO⁻ gives HC≡CH + 2CO₂ + 2e⁻ — option (c). Ethene (a) comes from potassium succinate, which has a saturated CH₂–CH₂ unit.

questions.stem_md: A student has four five-carbon hydrocarbons with boiling points of 27.8, 30.0, 36.1 and 40.2 °C: pent-1-yne, pent-1-ene, pentane and 2-methylbutane. Which sequence lists them in increasing order of boiling point?
questions.solution_md: The branched isomer 2-methylbutane (27.8 °C) boils lowest because it is more compact; pent-1-ene (30.0 °C) is a little below pentane (36.1 °C); the linear, easily polarised pent-1-yne (40.2 °C) boils highest — option (b). Option (a) is the exact reverse; (c) and (d) each swap two neighbours.

questions.stem_md: Methane from natural gas is passed through an electric arc at about 1773 K, and the hot gases are cooled very rapidly. The two products are:
questions.solution_md: 2CH₄ → C₂H₂ + 3H₂ at about 1773 K; rapid quenching stops the ethyne from decomposing into carbon and hydrogen — option (c). Ethene (a) and ethane (b) are not the main products, and carbon monoxide (d) forms only in the partial-oxidation route, which needs oxygen.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best explains why the hydrogen atoms of ethyne are more acidic than those of ethene?

options.text_md: The C–H bond of ethyne uses an sp orbital, which has more s character than the sp² orbital of ethene
The C≡C bond of ethyne is longer than the C=C bond of ethene
Ethyne has more hydrogen atoms than ethene has
The π bonds of ethyne are formed by overlap of s orbitals

questions.solution_md: An sp orbital is 50% s, an sp² orbital 33.3% s. The more s character, the closer the electrons are held to the nucleus, so the carbon is more electronegative and the HC≡C⁻ ion is more stable — option (a). The C≡C bond is shorter, not longer (b); ethyne has fewer hydrogens (c); π bonds come from p orbitals (d).

questions.stem_md: A student ranks the C–H bonds of ethane, ethene and ethyne by the s character (25, 33.3 and 50 per cent) of the carbon orbital that holds the hydrogen. The order of increasing acidity is:
questions.solution_md: Acidity increases with the s character of the carbon orbital: sp³ (25%) < sp² (33.3%) < sp (50%), so ethane < ethene < ethyne — option (b). Option (a) is the reverse order; (c) and (d) put the sp² compound out of sequence.

questions.stem_md: Sodium amide in liquid ammonia is added separately to four hydrocarbons in four flasks. Ammonia is liberated and a sodium salt is formed in the flask containing:
questions.solution_md: NH₂⁻ removes a proton only from a sufficiently acidic C–H, and among these only a terminal alkyne has one: CH₃CH₂C≡CH + NaNH₂ → CH₃CH₂C≡CNa + NH₃ — option (d). But-2-yne (a) has no ≡C–H and the alkene (b) and alkane (c) are far too weakly acidic.

questions.stem_md: Two isomeric alkynes A and B have the formula C₅H₈. Only A gives a white precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate, and boiling A with hot acidified potassium permanganate gives butanoic acid and carbon dioxide. A is:
questions.solution_md: The precipitate shows that A is a terminal alkyne. Hot KMnO₄ turns the ≡CH carbon into CO₂ and the other carbon into COOH, so CH₃CH₂CH₂–C≡CH gives CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH (butanoic acid) + CO₂: pent-1-yne — option (b). 3-Methylbut-1-yne (c) would give 2-methylpropanoic acid, pent-2-yne (a) gives no precipitate and the diene (d) is not an alkyne.

questions.stem_md: Propyne is passed into an excess of hydrogen chloride in the presence of mercury(II) chloride. The final product is:
questions.solution_md: The first HCl adds by Markownikoff's rule to give 2-chloropropene, CH₃C(Cl)=CH₂; the second HCl adds to the same carbon again, giving CH₃CCl₂CH₃, 2,2-dichloropropane — option (d). 2-Chloropropene (c) is only the intermediate; (a) and (b) put the chlorine on the wrong carbons.

questions.stem_md: Hex-3-yne is warmed with dilute sulphuric acid containing mercury(II) sulphate. The single carbonyl compound formed is:
questions.solution_md: OH adds to one of the two identical triple-bond carbons to give the enol CH₃CH₂CH=C(OH)CH₂CH₃, which shifts to the ketone CH₃CH₂CH₂–CO–CH₂CH₃, hexan-3-one — option (d). No aldehyde (a) forms because neither carbon is terminal, hexan-2-one (b) would need the triple bond at C-2 and the dione (c) is an ozonolysis-type product.

questions.stem_md: Oct-4-yne is shaken with hydrogen over palladium on calcium carbonate that has been poisoned with quinoline. The main product is:
questions.solution_md: Poisoned palladium (Lindlar's catalyst) adds one molecule of H₂ on the same face of the triple bond (syn addition) and stops at the alkene: cis-oct-4-ene — option (c). The trans isomer (a) needs sodium in liquid ammonia, octane (b) needs an unpoisoned catalyst and the position of the double bond cannot move (d).

questions.stem_md: Hept-3-yne, CH₃CH₂C≡CCH₂CH₂CH₃, is boiled with hot acidified potassium permanganate. The organic products are:
questions.solution_md: Hot KMnO₄ cleaves the triple bond and oxidises each carbon to COOH: the CH₃CH₂– side gives propanoic acid and the CH₃CH₂CH₂– side gives butanoic acid — option (b). Only one acid would form from a symmetrical alkyne (a); the aldehydes (c) are over-oxidised and the dione (d) would need controlled ozonolysis.

questions.stem_md: Propyne vapour is passed through an iron tube heated to redness, and the cyclic trimer is collected. The aromatic product is:
questions.solution_md: Three propyne molecules (C₃H₄) join to give C₉H₁₂ with a benzene ring; each ring carbon comes from an alternate carbon of the chain, so the three methyl groups end up on alternate carbons: 1,3,5-trimethylbenzene — option (a). Methylbenzene has only 7 carbons (b) and benzene (d) is the product from ethyne.

questions.stem_md: Ethane, ethene and ethyne are burnt in air from three identical burners. Ethyne gives by far the sootiest flame because:

options.text_md: its percentage of carbon by mass is the highest, so combustion in air is the least complete
it has the highest enthalpy of combustion per mole
it is the only one of the three that is unsaturated

questions.solution_md: The percentages of carbon are 80.0 (ethane), 85.7 (ethene) and 92.3 (ethyne). With a limited air supply, the carbon-rich compound leaves the most unburnt carbon as soot — option (a). Ethyne's enthalpy of combustion per mole (about 1300 kJ) is the lowest of the three (b), it does have C–H bonds (c) and ethene is also unsaturated (d).

questions.stem_md: Ethyne is bubbled slowly into a solution of bromine in tetrachloromethane until exactly one mole of bromine has been used for each mole of ethyne. The main product is:
questions.solution_md: One mole of Br₂ adds across one of the two π bonds: HC≡CH + Br₂ → CHBr=CHBr, 1,2-dibromoethene — option (c). A second mole would give the tetrabromo compound (a); (b) would need a saturated product from a double bond and (d) contains only one Br.

questions.stem_md: Which single reagent gives a different observation with but-1-yne and but-2-yne?
questions.solution_md: Only but-1-yne has a ≡C–H group, so only it gives a white precipitate of silver butynide with ammoniacal AgNO₃ — option (d). Both alkynes decolourise bromine water (a) and Baeyer's reagent (b) and both take up hydrogen over nickel (c).

questions.stem_md: A gas decolourises bromine water and cold dilute alkaline potassium permanganate, but gives no precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate. The gas could be:
questions.solution_md: Decolourising both reagents shows an unsaturated compound, and no precipitate rules out a terminal alkyne: propene — option (d). Propyne (a) and ethyne (c) would both give a precipitate, and propane (b) would not decolourise bromine water.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ethyne liberates hydrogen gas when sodium metal is added to it under suitable conditions.

**Reason (R):** The C–H bond of ethyne uses an sp orbital with 50% s character, which makes its hydrogen weakly acidic.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: the sp carbon holds the C–H pair tightly, so the hydrogen is displaced by sodium as 2HC≡CH + 2Na → 2HC≡CNa + H₂ — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Calcium carbide reacts with cold water to give ethyne and calcium hydroxide.

**Reason (R):** Calcium carbide is manufactured by heating lime and coke in an electric arc furnace.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. The hydrolysis of CaC₂ happens because the carbide ion C₂²⁻ is a strong base that takes protons from water; the way carbide is manufactured has no bearing on this, so R does not explain A — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Hydration of propyne with mercury(II) sulphate and dilute sulphuric acid gives propanone.

**Reason (R):** The enol formed first is stable and can be isolated from the reaction mixture.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: the enol CH₂=C(OH)CH₃ is unstable and rearranges at once to the keto form, propanone (tautomerism) — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Hydrogenation of but-2-yne over Lindlar's catalyst gives trans-but-2-ene.

**Reason (R):** Lindlar's catalyst is palladium on charcoal without any poison, so the reduction continues to the alkane.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are false: Lindlar's catalyst is palladium on calcium carbonate, poisoned with lead acetate and quinoline, and it stops at the cis alkene by syn addition — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The carbon–carbon bond in ethyne is shorter than the carbon–carbon bond in ethene.

**Reason (R):** The two π bonds of ethyne are formed by head-on overlap of sp hybrid orbitals.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true (120 pm against 134 pm). R is false: π bonds are formed by the sideways overlap of unhybridised p orbitals; head-on overlap of sp orbitals gives the σ bond — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Propyne adds two moles of hydrogen bromide to give 2,2-dibromopropane.

**Reason (R):** Propyne is a gas at room temperature.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true (propyne boils at −23.2 °C). The product follows from Markownikoff addition twice to the same carbon, which has nothing to do with the physical state — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? All four atoms of an ethyne molecule lie on one straight line because each carbon atom is sp hybridised.
questions.solution_md: True. The two sp orbitals of each carbon point in opposite directions (180°), so H–C≡C–H is linear.

questions.stem_md: True or false? But-2-yne gives a white precipitate when it is passed into ammoniacal silver nitrate solution.
questions.solution_md: False. But-2-yne has no hydrogen on a triple-bonded carbon, so it cannot form an acetylide; only terminal alkynes such as but-1-yne give the precipitate.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Every alkyne other than ethyne gives a ketone, not an aldehyde, on hydration with mercury(II) sulphate and dilute sulphuric acid.
questions.solution_md: True. OH adds to the carbon with fewer hydrogens (or to either carbon of an internal alkyne), so the carbonyl carbon always has two carbon neighbours; only ethyne gives an aldehyde, ethanal.

questions.stem_md: The unstable first product of the hydration of an alkyne, which has an OH group on a doubly bonded carbon, is called an ___.
questions.solution_md: An **enol**, which shifts to the carbonyl compound.

questions.stem_md: The carbon atoms joined by the triple bond in ethyne are ___ hybridised.
questions.solution_md: **sp** hybridised: two σ bonds in a line and two p orbitals for the two π bonds.

questions.stem_md: Ethyne forms benzene when passed through a red-hot iron tube kept at about ___ K.
Match each reaction of ethyne in Column I with its main product in Column II.

options.text_md: Ethyne with one mole of HCl and HgCl₂
Ethyne with water, HgSO₄ and dilute H₂SO₄
Ethyne with sodium amide in liquid ammonia
Ethyne through a red-hot iron tube

questions.solution_md: One mole of HCl adds once to give chloroethene; hydration gives the enol and then ethanal; NaNH₂ removes the acidic hydrogen to give the acetylide; trimerisation gives benzene.

questions.stem_md: Match each source of ethyne in Column I with the key reagent or condition in Column II.

match_right.text_md: Electric arc at about 1773 K, then quenching

questions.solution_md: Carbide is hydrolysed by water; a vicinal dihalide loses two HBr with alkali and amide; Kolbe electrolysis of the dicarboxylate gives ethyne; methane is cracked in an arc and quenched.

questions.stem_md: A caver in Meghalaya charges a lamp with 16.0 g of technical calcium carbide that contains 80.0% CaC₂ by mass; water drips on it until all the CaC₂ has reacted. What volume of ethyne, in litres at STP, is released? (Ca = 40, C = 12; molar volume 22.4 L)
questions.solution_md: Pure CaC₂ $= 16.0 \times 80.0/100 = 12.8\ \text{g}$, so $n = 12.8 \div 64 = 0.200\ \text{mol}$. From $\ce{CaC2 + 2H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2}$, 1 mol gives 1 mol of ethyne: $V = 0.200 \times 22.4 = 4.48\ \text{L}$.

marking_scheme.step: Mass of pure CaC₂ = 12.8 g and n = 0.200 mol

questions.stem_md: A student in a polymer laboratory bubbles 5.20 g of ethyne into excess bromine in tetrachloromethane and isolates 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane with a yield of 75.0%. What mass of the product, in grams, is obtained? (C = 12, H = 1, Br = 80)
questions.solution_md: $\ce{HC#CH + 2Br2 -> CHBr2CHBr2}$. $n(\text{C}_2\text{H}_2) = 5.20 \div 26 = 0.200\ \text{mol}$ and $M(\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{Br}_4) = 346\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$, so the theoretical mass is $0.200 \times 346 = 69.2\ \text{g}$. At 75.0% yield, $m = 69.2 \times 75.0/100 = 51.9\ \text{g}$.

questions.stem_md: A gas sample of 50.0 mL, a mixture of ethane and ethyne, needs 60.0 mL of hydrogen for complete hydrogenation over a nickel catalyst (all volumes at the same temperature and pressure). What volume of ethane, in mL, does the sample contain?
questions.solution_md: Ethane does not react; $\ce{HC#CH + 2H2 -> CH3CH3}$ takes 2 volumes of H₂ per volume of ethyne. $V(\text{ethyne}) = 60.0 \div 2 = 30.0\ \text{mL}$, so $V(\text{ethane}) = 50.0 - 30.0 = 20.0\ \text{mL}$.

marking_scheme.step: 2 volumes of H₂ per volume of ethyne gives 30.0 mL ethyne

questions.stem_md: Describe the bonding in an ethyne molecule: give the hybridisation of carbon, the kinds of bond between the two carbons and the shape of the molecule.

answer.model_answer_md: Each carbon is sp hybridised. The two carbons are joined by one σ bond (head-on overlap of sp orbitals) and two π bonds (sideways overlap of the two pairs of unhybridised p orbitals, in perpendicular planes). The other sp orbital of each carbon bonds to hydrogen, so the molecule is linear, H–C≡C–H, with an angle of 180°.

questions.solution_md: sp; one σ and two π; linear.

marking_scheme.step: sp hybridisation; one σ and two π bonds

questions.stem_md: The carbon–carbon bond lengths in ethane, ethene and ethyne are 154 pm, 134 pm and 120 pm. Explain this trend.

answer.model_answer_md: As the number of bonds between the carbons rises from one to two to three, more electron density lies between the nuclei and pulls them closer, so the bond shortens. In addition, the carbon orbital of the σ bond has more s character (sp³ 25%, sp² 33%, sp 50%), and an s orbital is smaller and nearer the nucleus, which shortens the bond further.

questions.solution_md: More bonds; more s character.

marking_scheme.step: More bonding electrons between the nuclei pull the carbons closer
Greater s character gives a shorter σ bond

questions.stem_md: Write balanced equations for (i) the formation of calcium carbide from quicklime and coke in an electric furnace and (ii) the production of ethyne from calcium carbide.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) $\ce{CaO + 3C -> CaC2 + CO}$ (about 2273 K). (ii) $\ce{CaC2 + 2H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2}$.

questions.solution_md: Two equations.

questions.stem_md: Write the equation for the preparation of propyne from 1,2-dibromopropane with excess alcoholic potassium hydroxide, and explain why two moles of the alkali are needed for each mole of the dihalide.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{CH3CHBrCH2Br + 2KOH -> CH3C#CH + 2KBr + 2H2O}$. Each KOH removes one molecule of HBr: the first gives a bromopropene and the second removes another H and Br to form the triple bond, so two moles are needed.

questions.solution_md: Equation; two HBr removed.

marking_scheme.step: Two moles of HBr are eliminated, one per KOH

questions.stem_md: Aqueous potassium maleate is electrolysed in a cell with inert electrodes. Write the overall equation and name the products at the anode and at the cathode.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{KOOCCH=CHCOOK + 2H2O -> HC#CH + 2CO2 + H2 + 2KOH}$. At the anode, the carboxylate ions lose electrons and CO₂ to give ethyne together with carbon dioxide; at the cathode, water is reduced to hydrogen gas and hydroxide ions (KOH).

questions.solution_md: Overall equation; anode ethyne and CO₂; cathode H₂.

marking_scheme.step: Ethyne and CO₂ at the anode; H₂ at the cathode

questions.stem_md: Account for the order of acidity ethyne > ethene > ethane in terms of the hybridisation of carbon.

answer.model_answer_md: The acidity depends on the s character of the carbon orbital in the C–H bond: sp in ethyne (50%), sp² in ethene (33.3%) and sp³ in ethane (25%). An orbital with more s character is nearer the nucleus, so the carbon is more electronegative, the proton is lost more easily and the carbanion formed is more stable.

questions.solution_md: sp > sp² > sp³ in s character.

marking_scheme.step: More s character: carbanion more stable, proton lost more easily

questions.stem_md: Write equations for the reaction of ethyne with (i) ammoniacal silver nitrate and (ii) ammoniacal cuprous chloride, and give the colour of each precipitate.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) $\ce{HC#CH + 2AgNO3 + 2NH4OH -> AgC#CAg + 2NH4NO3 + 2H2O}$, a white precipitate of silver acetylide. (ii) $\ce{HC#CH + Cu2Cl2 + 2NH4OH -> CuC#CCu + 2NH4Cl + 2H2O}$, a red precipitate of copper acetylide.

questions.solution_md: Two equations; white and red.

marking_scheme.step: Silver acetylide equation and white colour
Copper acetylide equation and red colour

questions.stem_md: Write equations for the cyclic polymerisation of (i) ethyne and (ii) propyne, giving the conditions and naming the products.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) $\ce{3C2H2 -> C6H6}$ when ethyne is passed through a red-hot iron tube at about 873 K; the product is benzene. (ii) $\ce{3CH3C#CH -> C9H12}$ under the same conditions; the product is 1,3,5-trimethylbenzene.

questions.solution_md: Two equations with names.

questions.stem_md: Describe how ethyne is converted into ethanal. Name the reagents, the unstable intermediate and the kind of isomerism by which the intermediate changes into the product.

answer.model_answer_md: Ethyne is warmed with dilute H₂SO₄ and HgSO₄. Water adds to give the enol ethenol, $\ce{CH2=CHOH}$, which is unstable and rearranges at once to ethanal, $\ce{CH3CHO}$. The change of enol into carbonyl compound is tautomerism (keto–enol).

questions.solution_md: HgSO₄/H₂SO₄; enol; tautomerism.

questions.stem_md: Write the condensed structures and IUPAC names of all the alkynes of formula C₅H₈, and state which of them give a white precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate.

answer.model_answer_md: CH₃CH₂CH₂C≡CH, pent-1-yne; CH₃CH₂C≡CCH₃, pent-2-yne; (CH₃)₂CHC≡CH, 3-methylbut-1-yne. Pent-1-yne and 3-methylbut-1-yne are terminal alkynes (they have a ≡C–H group) and give the white precipitate of the silver acetylide; pent-2-yne has no hydrogen on a triple-bonded carbon and gives none.

questions.solution_md: Three isomers; two terminal.

questions.stem_md: Ethyne made from technical calcium carbide has a garlic-like smell. Write the equation for its formation, say what causes the smell, and name a reagent that purifies the gas.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{CaC2 + 2H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2}$. Impurities in the coke and lime form traces of phosphine, hydrogen sulphide and ammonia in the carbide, and these gases are released with the ethyne; phosphine causes the garlic-like smell. They are removed by passing the gas through acidified copper(II) sulphate solution (or acidified potassium dichromate).

questions.solution_md: Equation; phosphine; acidified CuSO₄.

marking_scheme.step: Smell due to phosphine (and H₂S, NH₃) from impurities

questions.stem_md: Write equations for the reaction of propyne with (i) sodium amide in liquid ammonia and (ii) ammoniacal silver nitrate, and explain why but-2-yne does not react with either reagent.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) $\ce{CH3C#CH + NaNH2 -> CH3C#CNa + NH3}$. (ii) $\ce{CH3C#CH + AgNO3 + NH4OH -> CH3C#CAg + NH4NO3 + H2O}$, a white precipitate. But-2-yne, CH₃C≡CCH₃, has no hydrogen on a triple-bonded carbon, so it has no acidic C–H to lose and cannot form an acetylide.

questions.solution_md: Two equations; no ≡C–H.

questions.stem_md: Ethyne is treated with an excess of hydrogen chloride in the presence of mercury(II) chloride. Write the equations for the two successive additions, name the intermediate and the final product, and state the rule that fixes the position of the second chlorine atom.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{HC#CH + HCl -> CH2=CHCl}$ (chloroethene), then $\ce{CH2=CHCl + HCl -> CH3CHCl2}$ (1,1-dichloroethane). The second chlorine goes to the carbon that already carries one, following Markownikoff's rule: the negative part of HX adds to the carbon with fewer hydrogens, and the chlorine stabilises the positive charge on its own carbon.

questions.solution_md: Two equations; geminal product; Markownikoff.

questions.stem_md: Explain, using the structure of the enol, why the hydration of propyne gives propanone and not propanal.

answer.model_answer_md: Water adds by Markownikoff's rule: H goes to the terminal carbon, which has more hydrogens, and OH to the middle carbon, giving the enol CH₂=C(OH)CH₃ (prop-1-en-2-ol). The enol is unstable and shifts its hydrogen from O to the terminal carbon, giving the carbonyl compound CH₃–CO–CH₃, propanone. For propanal the OH would have to be on the terminal carbon, which Markownikoff addition does not give.

questions.solution_md: Markownikoff; enol; tautomerism.

marking_scheme.step: OH on the middle carbon by Markownikoff's rule

questions.stem_md: Give the organic products formed when (i) hex-2-yne is boiled with hot acidified potassium permanganate and (ii) ethyne is burnt in a plentiful supply of oxygen, and name one industrial use of the second reaction.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Hot KMnO₄ cleaves the triple bond and oxidises each carbon to a carboxylic acid: ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, and butanoic acid, CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH. (ii) $\ce{2C2H2 + 5O2 -> 4CO2 + 2H2O}$; the very hot oxy-acetylene flame (about 3000 °C) is used for welding and cutting metals.

questions.solution_md: Ethanoic and butanoic acids; combustion; welding.

marking_scheme.step: Welding or cutting as the use

questions.stem_md: A welder's cylinder releases 2.80 L of ethyne, measured at STP, which is burnt completely in oxygen. Write the balanced equation and calculate the volume of oxygen consumed at STP and the mass of carbon dioxide formed. (C = 12, O = 16; molar volume 22.4 L)

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{2C2H2 + 5O2 -> 4CO2 + 2H2O}$. $n(\text{C}_2\text{H}_2) = 2.80 \div 22.4 = 0.125$ mol. Oxygen: $2.5 \times 0.125 = 0.3125$ mol, so $V = 7.00$ L. Carbon dioxide: $2 \times 0.125 = 0.250$ mol, so mass $= 0.250 \times 44 = 11.0$ g.

questions.solution_md: Equation; oxygen 7.00 L; CO₂ 11.0 g.

questions.stem_md: Calculate the percentage of carbon by mass in ethane, ethene and ethyne (C = 12, H = 1), and use the values to explain why ethyne burns with a sooty flame in air but gives a very hot, soot-free flame when burnt in pure oxygen.

answer.model_answer_md: Ethane C₂H₆: 24/30 × 100 = 80.0%; ethene C₂H₄: 24/28 × 100 = 85.7%; ethyne C₂H₂: 24/26 × 100 = 92.3%. Ethyne is the richest in carbon, and the air supply of an ordinary burner is not enough to oxidise all of it, so unburnt carbon glows as a sooty flame. In pure oxygen the supply is ample, so combustion is complete: 2C₂H₂ + 5O₂ → 4CO₂ + 2H₂O, and the heat evolved gives the very hot oxy-acetylene flame.

questions.solution_md: Percentages 80.0, 85.7, 92.3; incomplete combustion in air.

marking_scheme.step: Highest carbon content leads to incomplete combustion in air
Complete combustion in oxygen gives a hot, clean flame

questions.stem_md: Three gas jars in a store-room are labelled only A, B and C. They contain ethane, ethene and ethyne in some order. Describe a sequence of tests, with the observations, that identifies each gas.

answer.model_answer_md: Pass each gas through ammoniacal silver nitrate solution: the gas that gives a white precipitate is ethyne (a terminal alkyne). Shake the other two with bromine water: the one that decolourises it is ethene; the one that causes no change is ethane (an alkane does not react). Baeyer's reagent can be used in place of bromine water in the second test.

questions.solution_md: Ammoniacal AgNO₃ then bromine water.

marking_scheme.step: Ammoniacal AgNO₃: white precipitate identifies ethyne

questions.stem_md: Ethyne reacts with sodium amide but gives no useful acetylide with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Using the approximate pKa values of ethyne (25) and water (15.7), explain this, and say what you would observe on adding sodium metal to ethyne in liquid ammonia.

answer.model_answer_md: A base can deprotonate an acid effectively only if the acid it forms is weaker than the one it removes the proton from. Water (pKa 15.7) is a much stronger acid than ethyne (pKa 25), so the OH⁻ ion is not basic enough and the equilibrium lies on the side of ethyne and OH⁻. The amide ion is the conjugate base of ammonia, a far weaker acid, so it removes the proton completely. With sodium in liquid ammonia, bubbles of hydrogen are seen as sodium acetylide forms.

questions.solution_md: Ethyne is a weaker acid than water; NH₂⁻ is a stronger base.

marking_scheme.step: Compare the acidity of ethyne and water
NH₂⁻ is a stronger base than OH⁻

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the bonding in ethyne, giving the hybridisation of carbon, the number of σ and π bonds in the molecule and its shape. [2]

(b) The carbon–carbon bond lengths are 154 pm in ethane, 134 pm in ethene and 120 pm in ethyne. Which bond is the strongest, and why is it the shortest? [1]

(c) Write the structures and IUPAC names of the two alkynes of formula C₄H₆ and say why neither has cis–trans isomers. [2]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Each carbon is sp hybridised; ethyne has 3 σ bonds (two C–H and one C–C) and 2 π bonds, and is linear (180°). (b) The C≡C bond is the strongest and shortest: three bonding pairs (one σ and two π) hold the carbons together, and the sp orbital of the σ bond has the most s character. (c) CH₃CH₂C≡CH, but-1-yne, and CH₃C≡CCH₃, but-2-yne. Cis–trans isomerism needs two different groups on each carbon of a double bond in a planar arrangement; each triple-bonded carbon carries only one other group, on a straight line.

questions.solution_md: sp; 3σ, 2π; strongest; two isomers; no cis–trans.

marking_scheme.step: (a) sp hybridisation; 3 σ and 2 π bonds
(b) strongest and shortest because of three bonding pairs and s character
(c) no cis–trans: one group per carbon on a straight line

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write balanced equations for the manufacture of ethyne from limestone, coke and water, through calcium oxide and calcium carbide. [2]

(b) State how ethyne is obtained from natural gas, with the equation and conditions. [1]

(c) Write the equation for the preparation of propyne from 1,1-dibromopropane, and state the reagent and the number of moles of it that are needed. [2]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $\ce{CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2}$; $\ce{CaO + 3C -> CaC2 + CO}$ (electric furnace, about 2273 K); $\ce{CaC2 + 2H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2}$. (b) Methane is heated in an electric arc to about 1773 K and quenched rapidly: $\ce{2CH4 -> C2H2 + 3H2}$. (c) $\ce{CH3CH2CHBr2 + 2KOH -> CH3C#CH + 2KBr + 2H2O}$; alcoholic KOH, 2 mol per mole of dibromide.

questions.solution_md: Carbide route; arc process; geminal dihalide.

questions.stem_md:
(a) The s character of the carbon orbital in the C–H bond is 25% in ethane, 33.3% in ethene and 50% in ethyne. Explain how this accounts for the acidity of ethyne. [2]

(b) Write equations for the reaction of ethyne with sodium and with ammoniacal silver nitrate. [2]

(c) How can ethyne be regenerated from the silver compound? [1]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The orbital with more s character is closer to the nucleus, so the sp carbon is more electronegative than sp² or sp³ carbon; it holds the bonding pair more strongly, the hydrogen is released as H⁺ more easily, and the HC≡C⁻ ion is stabilised. (b) $\ce{2HC#CH + 2Na -> 2HC#CNa + H2}$ and $\ce{HC#CH + 2AgNO3 + 2NH4OH -> AgC#CAg + 2NH4NO3 + 2H2O}$. (c) Treat the (moist) precipitate with dilute nitric acid, which protonates the acetylide and gives back ethyne.

questions.solution_md: s character; two equations; dilute HNO₃.

marking_scheme.step: (a) more s character, nearer the nucleus, more electronegative

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the reagents by which but-2-yne can be converted into (i) cis-but-2-ene, (ii) trans-but-2-ene and (iii) butane. [2]

(b) But-1-yne is warmed with mercury(II) sulphate and dilute sulphuric acid. Write the structure of the enol first formed and the final product, and name the type of isomerism between them. [2]

(c) Name the product when propyne reacts with an excess of hydrogen bromide. [1]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) (i) H₂ with Lindlar's catalyst (Pd on CaCO₃, poisoned); (ii) sodium in liquid ammonia; (iii) H₂ in excess with Ni (or Pt, Pd). (b) The enol is CH₂=C(OH)CH₂CH₃ (OH on the carbon with fewer hydrogens); it rearranges to butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, the change being tautomerism. (c) Two moles of HBr add to the same carbon by Markownikoff's rule, giving 2,2-dibromopropane.

questions.solution_md: Lindlar; Na/NH₃; Ni; enol and butanone; 2,2-dibromopropane.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Lindlar and sodium in liquid ammonia

questions.stem_md:
A hydrocarbon X of molecular formula C₆H₁₀ gives a white precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate. On boiling with hot acidified potassium permanganate it gives pentanoic acid and carbon dioxide.

(a) Deduce the structure of X and name it. [2]

(b) An isomer Y of X gives no precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate, and hot permanganate converts it into ethanoic acid and butanoic acid. Identify Y. [1]

(c) Give the product when X is hydrated with HgSO₄ and dilute H₂SO₄. [1]

(d) What volume of hydrogen at STP is needed to convert 4.10 g of X completely into the alkane? (C = 12, H = 1; molar volume 22.4 L) [1]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The precipitate shows a terminal alkyne; the acid and CO₂ mean CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂–C≡CH is oxidised to CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂COOH + CO₂. X is hex-1-yne. (b) Y has no ≡C–H and splits into a 2-carbon and a 4-carbon acid: CH₃–C≡C–CH₂CH₂CH₃, hex-2-yne. (c) OH adds to C-2, giving the enol which rearranges to hexan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃. (d) n(X) = 4.10 ÷ 82 = 0.050 mol; 2 mol of H₂ per mole of alkyne gives 0.100 mol, so V = 0.100 × 22.4 = 2.24 L.

questions.solution_md: Hex-1-yne; hex-2-yne; hexan-2-one; 2.24 L.

marking_scheme.step: (a) terminal alkyne with a straight chain; hex-1-yne

questions.stem_md:
Three colourless gases A, B and C are each one of ethane, ethene and ethyne. Each is tested in turn with three reagents, with the results below.

A: ammoniacal silver nitrate gives a white precipitate; bromine water is decolourised.
B: no precipitate; bromine water is decolourised; cold dilute alkaline permanganate is decolourised.
C: no precipitate; bromine water and permanganate are both unchanged.

(a) Identify A, B and C, giving a reason for each. [3]

(b) Write the equation for the reaction of A with an excess of bromine. [1]

(c) Why would bromine water alone not have been enough to separate A from B? [1]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) A is ethyne: the precipitate needs a terminal alkyne with an acidic ≡C–H. B is ethene: it is unsaturated (it decolourises both reagents) but has no acidic hydrogen. C is ethane: a saturated alkane does not react with any of the reagents. (b) $\ce{HC#CH + 2Br2 -> CHBr2CHBr2}$ (1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane). (c) Both ethyne and ethene decolourise bromine water, so only the silver nitrate test separates them.

questions.solution_md: A ethyne; B ethene; C ethane; tetrabromoethane.

marking_scheme.step: (c) both unsaturated gases decolourise bromine water
